key_terms.meaning: A P-T (or P-V-T) map of a pure substance showing solid, liquid and gas regions and the lines where two phases coexist
The single temperature and pressure where solid, liquid and vapour coexist in equilibrium; for water 273.16 K and 611.657 Pa
The highest temperature and pressure at which a liquid and its vapour can be told apart; above it only a supercritical fluid exists
The pressure at which a liquid and its vapour coexist at a given temperature; it rises with temperature and ends at the critical point
PV = nRT, where P is pressure (Pa), V volume (m³), n moles (mol), T absolute temperature (K) and R = 8.314 J/(mol·K)
A path at constant temperature; for an ideal gas ΔU = 0 and w = nRT ln(V₂/V₁)
A path with no heat transfer (q = 0); for an ideal gas P V^γ = constant with γ = Cp/Cv
A path following P V^n = constant; n = 0 is isobaric, n → ∞ is isochoric, n = γ is adiabatic
Z = 1 + B/V + C/V² + … or Z = 1 + B′P + C′P² + …; B is the second virial coefficient and carries the first correction for molecular interaction
(P + a/V̄²)(V̄ − b) = RT, where V̄ is molar volume, b is the excluded volume of the molecules and a/V̄² is the attractive pressure correction

key_terms.term: van der Waals constants from critical data
key_terms.meaning: a = 27R²Tc²/(64Pc) and b = RTc/(8Pc); the predicted Zc = 3/8 = 0.375 against about 0.27 for real fluids
Z = PV/(nRT); Z = 1 for an ideal gas, below 1 when attraction dominates and above 1 when molecular size dominates
Tr = T/Tc, Pr = P/Pc, Vr = V/Vc; dimensionless variables that make different fluids fall on common curves
Two fluids at the same Tr and Pr have the same Z, so one chart or correlation serves many gases
ω = −1 − log₁₀(Pr^sat) evaluated at Tr = 0.7; it measures how far a molecule departs from a simple spherical fluid
Heat that changes the temperature of a single phase without changing it; Q = n∫Cp dT or n C̄p ΔT
Heat absorbed or released at constant temperature during a phase change, such as ΔHvap at the boiling point
ΔH°rxn = Σνᵢ ΔH°f,i for products minus reactants, both at 298.15 K and 1 bar
d(ΔH°rxn)/dT = Σνᵢ Cp,i, which shifts a heat of reaction from one temperature to another
ΔHvap, the heat to convert one mole of saturated liquid to saturated vapour at the same temperature and pressure; it falls to zero at the critical point

takeaways: A pure fluid's state is fixed by two intensive variables once the phase is known, and the phase diagram shows which phase wins.
The ideal gas law is a limiting law at low pressure and high temperature; it fails whenever molecules are close together.
Each ideal-gas path (isothermal, adiabatic, isochoric, isobaric) has its own fixed work and heat relations that you should be able to write from memory.
The virial equation is a systematic correction that gets better as more coefficients are added; the van der Waals equation is a simple closed-form model that predicts a critical point.
The compressibility factor Z turns an unknown real gas into a number you can read from a generalized chart using Tr and Pr.
Real-gas behaviour is well organized: attraction makes Z < 1, size makes Z > 1, and most fluids sit near a common curve.
Heat effects come in three kinds — sensible, latent and chemical — and each has its own calculation route.
Kirchhoff's equation is what lets you take a table value at 298 K and use it at your reactor temperature.
bank_note: Long answers in this unit usually ask you to write the equation, name every symbol with units, then either derive a critical-property relation or use the correlation in a numerical part.

bank.q: State the ideal gas law and define the compressibility factor Z. List the two physical assumptions behind the ideal gas model and say which one fails first at high pressure.
outline: PV = nRT with P in Pa, V in m³, n in mol, T in K, R = 8.314 J/(mol·K)
Z = PV/(nRT), equal to 1 for an ideal gas
Assumptions: molecules have negligible volume, and no intermolecular forces
At high pressure the finite molecular volume dominates first and Z rises above 1

bank.q: Draw the P-T phase diagram of a pure substance and explain each region and each line. Mark triple point and critical point, and explain what happens on heating at constant pressure from below the triple point to above the critical point.
outline: Axes P (y) and T (x); regions solid, liquid, vapour
Sublimation curve, fusion curve, vaporization curve meeting at the triple point
Vaporization curve ends at the critical point
Heating at constant P crosses sublimation, then fusion, then vaporization
Above Tc no meniscus forms; only supercritical fluid

bank.q: Write the van der Waals equation and explain the physical meaning of the constants a and b. Show how the critical-point conditions (∂P/∂V)T = 0 and (∂²P/∂V²)T = 0 lead to a = 27R²Tc²/(64Pc) and b = RTc/(8Pc).
outline: (P + a/V̄²)(V̄ − b) = RT written out in P form
b corrects volume for molecular size; a/V̄² corrects pressure for attraction
Differentiate P with respect to V̄ at constant T and set both first and second derivatives to zero at the critical point
Solve the three equations for a, b in terms of Tc, Pc
State the consequence Zc = 3/8 and compare with real fluids near 0.27

bank.q: Explain the principle of corresponding states. Define Tr, Pr and the acentric factor, and state why a third parameter improves the correlation.
outline: Tr = T/Tc, Pr = P/Pc, Z plotted against Pr with Tr as parameter
Two-parameter statement: all fluids with same Tr and Pr have same Z
Acentric factor ω = −1 − log₁₀(Pr^sat) at Tr = 0.7
Simple spherical molecules like argon have ω near 0; larger or polar molecules have larger ω
Third parameter separates the families of curves

bank.q: One mole of an ideal gas at 300 K is compressed reversibly and isothermally from 1 bar to 10 bar. Calculate w, q, ΔU and ΔH, and state the sign convention used.
outline: Isothermal ideal gas gives ΔU = 0 and ΔH = 0
w = −nRT ln(V₂/V₁) = −nRT ln(P₁/P₂)
n = 1 mol, R = 8.314 J/(mol·K), T = 300 K, ratio 0.1
w = +5744 J (work done on the gas)
q = −5744 J, heat leaves the gas

bank.q: One mole of an ideal gas with Cp = 29.1 J/(mol·K) and Cv = 20.8 J/(mol·K) is compressed reversibly and adiabatically from 1 bar and 300 K to 5 bar. Find the final temperature and the work.
outline: γ = Cp/Cv = 1.40
T₂ = T₁ (P₂/P₁)^((γ−1)/γ)
w = ΔU = n Cv (T₂ − T₁)
q = 0 by definition of adiabatic

bank.q: Carbon dioxide has Tc = 304.2 K and Pc = 73.8 bar. Using the van der Waals equation, estimate the pressure exerted by 1 mol of CO₂ in a 0.5 L vessel at 300 K, and compare it with the ideal gas value.
outline: Convert V to m³ and Pc to Pa
a = 27R²Tc²/(64Pc), b = RTc/(8Pc) with numbers
Substitute into P = RT/(V−b) − a/V²
Ideal gas value P = nRT/V
Real pressure is lower because attraction dominates at this density; comment on the difference

bank.q: A gas has Tc = 400 K, Pc = 40 bar and ω = 0.2. Estimate its molar volume at 500 K and 20 bar using the generalized compressibility chart or the Pitzer correlation.
outline: Read Z⁰ and Z¹ and compute Z = Z⁰ + ωZ¹
Typical result around Z ≈ 0.95
V = ZRT/P with T in K and P in Pa
State units of the final volume in m³/mol

bank.q: Calculate the heat needed to raise 2 mol/s of nitrogen from 300 K to 700 K at 1 bar, using Cp = 31.15 − 0.01357(T/K) + 2.68×10⁻⁵(T/K)² − 1.17×10⁻⁸(T/K)³ J/(mol·K).
outline: Sensible heat at constant pressure: Q = n∫Cp dT
Integrate each term between 300 K and 700 K
Multiply by 2 mol/s and state the answer in W or kW
Note the assumption of ideal-gas Cp and no phase change
Mention that the same integral gives ΔH

bank.q: Liquid water at 373 K and 1 atm is fully vaporized. Using ΔHvap = 40.66 kJ/mol at 373 K, find the heat needed per kg of water, and explain why the temperature stays constant during vaporization.
outline: Moles per kg = 1000/18.015 = 55.5 mol
Latent heat goes into breaking intermolecular bonds, not kinetic energy
Therefore temperature is constant until all liquid disappears
Link to the enthalpy change of vaporization in steam tables

bank.q: Liquid water at 1 bar and 298 K is heated to 1 bar and 400 K. Sketch the T-S or P-V path, and calculate ΔH using sensible heat plus latent heat.
outline: Path: heat liquid to 373 K, vaporize at 373 K, superheat vapour to 400 K
ΔH = ∫Cp,liq dT + ΔHvap + ∫Cp,vap dT
Cp,liq ≈ 75.3 J/(mol·K)
State the value in kJ/mol and mention that tables give the same result

bank.q: Plot and compare Z against P at fixed T for (a) an ideal gas, (b) a gas following the truncated virial equation, and (c) a van der Waals gas. Explain the low-pressure limit in each case and why all three curves share the same initial slope at a given temperature.
outline: All curves start at Z = 1 as P → 0
Initial slope equals B′ or b − a/(RT) at constant T
van der Waals gives b − a/(RT); attraction term dominates at low T, so Z dips below 1
At high T, size wins and Z climbs above 1
Truncated virial is reliable only to moderate pressure; vdW loops unphysically near condensation
Conclude on which model to trust at what density

bank.q: A pipeline carries natural gas at 150 bar and 300 K. Compare the ideal gas, van der Waals, and generalized compressibility routes for sizing the pipe, and recommend one for a plant design, giving reasons.
outline: Ideal gas badly overestimates volume at 150 bar; quote a plausible Z well below 1 or above depending on T
van der Waals is easy but inaccurate near critical conditions
Generalized correlations with ω give the best accuracy without a full EOS
Pitzer or a cubic EOS such as Peng-Robinson is the usual design choice
Risk of wrong volume: capital cost of the pipe and flow capacity are both wrong
Also mention safety margins and the cost of an error

bank.q: The standard heat of a reaction is tabulated at 298.15 K. Explain how you would find the adiabatic reaction temperature of an industrial reactor operating at 700 K, and discuss which heat effects you must include.
outline: Use Kirchhoff's equation to shift ΔH°rxn to 700 K
Energy balance: heat released by reaction = sensible heat to raise products to T_ad
Include any latent heats if a phase change occurs
Include excess reactants and inerts in the Cp sum
Iterate on T_ad since Cp values depend on temperature
Discuss why actual reactor temperature is lower — heat losses, incomplete conversion, side reactions

bank.q: Relate the shape of a van der Waals P-V isotherm below Tc to the phase behaviour of a real fluid. Explain the Maxwell equal-area construction and why the experimental path is flat.
outline: Subcritical isotherm shows a maximum and a minimum with a loop
The loop region is unstable or metastable physically
Maxwell construction: horizontal line at Psat with equal areas above and below
Real fluid: liquid and vapour coexist at constant P while volume changes
Above Tc the loop vanishes and the isotherm has a single inflection at the critical point
Connect to the critical point conditions

glossary.def: A substance made of one chemical species, so its state needs only two independent intensive variables.
A property that does not depend on the amount of material, such as P or T.
The temperature above which a gas cannot be liquefied by pressure alone.
The pressure needed to liquefy a fluid at its critical temperature.
A fluid above both Tc and Pc, with properties between those of a liquid and a gas.
The condition where two phases coexist at equilibrium at a given T and P.
The number of independent intensive variables that must be fixed to describe a system; for a pure fluid, one on a phase boundary and two in a single-phase region.
A coefficient in the virial series; the second virial coefficient B carries the correction for pairs of molecules interacting.
An equation of state that is cubic in molar volume, such as the van der Waals, Redlich-Kwong or Peng-Robinson equation.
A path at constant pressure; for an ideal gas q = ΔH and w = −P ΔV.
A path at constant volume; no P-V work is done, so w = 0 and q = ΔU.
A path taken through a series of equilibrium states, giving the maximum work obtainable.
The heat needed to raise one mole by one kelvin at constant volume; Cv = (∂U/∂T)V.
The heat needed to raise one mole by one kelvin at constant pressure; Cp = (∂H/∂T)P.
H = U + PV, a state function convenient for constant-pressure processes.
The energy stored in the molecules of a system, excluding bulk kinetic and potential energy.
The difference between a real-fluid property and the ideal-gas value at the same T and P, used to apply generalized charts.
A graph of Z against Pr with lines of constant Tr, allowing Z to be read for any gas.
α = (1/V)(∂V/∂T)P, which measures how fast volume grows with temperature.
κ = −(1/V)(∂V/∂P)T, which measures how much volume shrinks as pressure rises.
A tabulated set of properties of water and steam, organized by saturation pressure or temperature and by superheat.
The final temperature reached when the heat of reaction is entirely absorbed by the products, with no heat loss.
The pure substance at 1 bar and a stated temperature, usually 298.15 K, used as the reference for heats of formation.
